+# Normalize a clock time like 3pm, 3:30 p.m., 15:30, noon, or "tomorrow at 9am"
+# to "HH:MM" or "tomorrow HH:MM". Fails for anything else, so GNU date never
+# gets to read input like "1h" as a timezone.
+normalize_clock_time() {
+  local words when prefix=""
+
+  read -r -a words <<<"${1,,}"
+  when="${words[*]}"
+
+  if [[ $when =~ ^tomorrow\ (.+)$ ]] || [[ $when =~ ^(.+)\ tomorrow$ ]]; then
+    prefix="tomorrow "
+    when=${BASH_REMATCH[1]}
+  fi
+  when=${when#at }
+
+  case $when in
+  noon) when="12:00" ;;
+  midnight) when="00:00" ;;
+  esac
+
+  if [[ $when =~ ^([0-9]{1,2}(:[0-9]{2})?)\ ?([ap])\.?m?\.?$ ]]; then
+    when="${BASH_REMATCH[1]} ${BASH_REMATCH[3]}m"
+  elif [[ ! $when =~ ^[0-9]{1,2}:[0-9]{2}$ ]]; then
+    return 1
+  fi
+
+  when=$(TZ=UTC date -d "2000-01-01 $when" +%H:%M 2>/dev/null) || return 1
+  echo "$prefix$when"
+}
+
+next_day() {
+  date -d "$1 12:00 tomorrow" +%F
+}
+
+# UTC offset a day before <day> <HH:MM>, i.e. before any daylight-saving change on that day.
+offset_before_day() {
+  date -d "@$(($(TZ=UTC date -d "$1 $2" +%s) - 86400))" +%z
+}
+
+# Epoch for a wall-clock HH:MM on a calendar day, resolving daylight-saving
+# edges the way JavaScript dates do so the timer matches the prompt's preview:
+# a skipped time is read at the offset in force before the jump, and a
+# repeated time takes its first occurrence (GNU date picks either, by zone).
+local_time_epoch() {
+  local day=$1 clock=$2 at_earlier_offset as_parsed
+
+  at_earlier_offset=$(date -d "$day $clock $(offset_before_day "$day" "$clock")" +%s 2>/dev/null) || return 1
+
+  if ! as_parsed=$(date -d "$day $clock" +%s 2>/dev/null); then
+    echo "$at_earlier_offset"
+  elif ((at_earlier_offset < as_parsed)) && [[ $(date -d "@$at_earlier_offset" '+%F %H:%M') == "$day $clock" ]]; then
+    echo "$at_earlier_offset"
+  else
+    echo "$as_parsed"
+  fi
+}
+
+# Epoch for a clock time at or after <now>, rolling a time that has already
+# passed today over to tomorrow.
+clock_time_epoch() {
+  local now=$1 clock day target
+
+  clock=$(normalize_clock_time "$2") || return 1
+  day=$(date -d "@$now" +%F)
+
+  if [[ $clock == tomorrow\ * ]]; then
+    local_time_epoch "$(next_day "$day")" "${clock#tomorrow }"
+    return
+  fi
+
+  target=$(local_time_epoch "$day" "$clock") || return 1
+  if ((target <= now)); then
+    local_time_epoch "$(next_day "$day")" "$clock"
+  else
+    echo "$target"
+  fi
+}

 # Reminders
 
-Omarchy has a built-in way to set simple reminders based on a countdown timer and with a message. You can do this via `Super + Ctrl + R`, seeing all the ones set via `Super + Ctrl + Alt + R`, and clearing all via `Super + Ctrl + Shift + R`. Everything also accessible via _Trigger > Reminder_. You can also use the cli with `omarchy reminder 7 'Tea ready'`.
+Omarchy has a built-in way to set simple reminders based on a countdown timer or a time of day, and with a message. You can do this via `Super + Ctrl + R`, seeing all the ones set via `Super + Ctrl + Alt + R`, and clearing all via `Super + Ctrl + Shift + R`. Everything also accessible via _Trigger > Reminder_. You can also use the cli with `omarchy reminder 7 'Tea ready'` or `omarchy reminder 3:30pm 'Call mom'`.
+
+The prompt takes minutes (`15`), hours and minutes (`1h30m`), or a time of day (`3:30pm`, `15:30`, `noon`, `tomorrow 9am`), and previews when the reminder will go off as you type. A time that has already passed today is set for tomorrow.
